title: Prompt Engineering & Structured Output
goal: Given a production stem about unpredictable review findings, fabricated extractions, or a manager proposing batch, pick the option that matches the documented principle instead of the trap.

steps.title: The review bot developers stopped reading
steps.lead: Your CI review bot posts findings on every PR. Six weeks in, the survey says developers are dismissing findings without reading them, and that half of them are wrong. Name the actual defect before you touch anything: the bot was told to check that comments are accurate and up to date, and that phrase is the defect. It is not the model, the temperature, or the context window.
points: The prompt names a quality to look for, not a boundary between what qualifies and what does not.
So TODO markers and simple descriptions get flagged, while comments describing behaviour the code no longer implements get missed.
This is the recurring stem shape for the whole domain: instructions exist, the output is unpredictable.
The tested distinction is categorical versus adjectival. A confidence adjective or a threshold in an option means distractor.
steps.caption: Left is an adjective; right is a boundary. Only the right one tells the bot what qualifies.
steps.takeaway: An undefined criterion is the bug. Vague instructions do not become precise by adding more of them.
steps.inshort: The bug is the instruction, not the model: 'accurate and up to date' names a quality, not a boundary, so the bot flags everything and misses what matters.
steps.why: The stem describes unpredictable output from instructions that already exist; the tested distinction is categorical versus adjectival, so any confidence adjective or threshold in an option is a distractor.
steps.contrast: Rewriting the prompt to say 'be more accurate', or adding a confidence threshold, both of which ask the model to supply judgement it does not have.
steps.exam: Recurring stem shape for the domain: instructions exist, output is unpredictable. Name the layer before the fix.

steps.title: What to flag, what to report, what to skip
steps.lead: For every judgement the model has to make, define what qualifies, what does not qualify, and show the boundary with examples. That is what turns a quality adjective into an operational test. The structure is mandatory: what to flag, what to report, what to skip.
points: Flag when a comment's claimed behaviour contradicts what the code actually does.
Do not flag comments that are merely incomplete or could be more detailed. Explain adversarial cases in the same structure.
Anchor severity levels with real code examples, not prose. Prose severity drifts across runs; code anchors do not.
A high false-positive rate in one category destroys trust in all categories, including the accurate ones.
The fix is to temporarily disable the noisy category while you improve its criteria, then re-enable it.
steps.caption: Read left to right: a finding only exists because one of these three lists claims it.
steps.takeaway: Flag X, report Y, skip Z. Disable the noisy category rather than tightening it in place.
steps.inshort: Turn every judgement into an operational test: what to flag, what to report, what to skip, with adversarial cases and code anchors for severity.
steps.why: The exam wants the categorical structure, not a nicer adjective; prose severity drifts across runs while code anchors do not.
steps.contrast: A five-level severity rubric written in prose, or tightening the noisy category in place instead of disabling it.
steps.exam: Flag X, report Y, skip Z. A high false-positive rate in one category destroys trust in all of them.

steps.title: Gate: trust collapse by category
steps.lead: Now the numbers version of that bot. Once one noisy category is in the report, your accurate categories stop getting read too, and that detail decides the answer.
steps.caption: Read the middle column: the 52% and 48% rows destroy trust in the 8% row, so those categories come off.

ask.q: False-positive rates vary widely by finding category: security and correctness findings run at 8%, performance at 18%, style and naming at 52%, documentation at 48%. Developer surveys show growing distrust, with many now dismissing findings without reading them, saying "half are wrong". Which approach is most effective?
options: Temporarily disable the high-false-positive categories and keep only the high-precision categories while their prompts are improved.
Keep all categories enabled but display a confidence score with each finding so developers can decide what to investigate.
Keep all categories enabled and add few-shot examples to improve accuracy for each category over the next few weeks.
Apply a uniform strictness reduction across all categories to bring the overall false-positive rate down.
ask.why: High false positives in some categories destroy trust in the accurate ones, so the immediate fix is to remove the noisy categories from output rather than leaving them on screen while accuracy improves slowly. Disabling also buys the space to iterate on those criteria before re-enabling them. A uniform strictness reduction trades away the true positives in the accurate security and correctness categories.

steps.takeaway: Disable the noisy category, improve its criteria, re-enable. Do not tighten in place.

steps.title: Better-defined reviewing, not less aggressive
steps.inshort: The same reviewer went from 47 findings per PR to three by replacing vague adjectives with explicit flag, severity and skip rules, not by becoming less aggressive.
steps.lead: Same repository, same reviewer, one prompt change. Before, every PR came back with 47 findings: variable-naming opinions, style the linter does not enforce, and sub-5-millisecond micro-optimisations. After, the same reviewer reports three findings, a SQL injection, a missing error handler and a race condition, and every one is real and fixable. Nobody made it less aggressive; they made it better-defined.
points: Adding words creates more surface area for ambiguity, not less. A 500-word essay and a 1000-line prompt leave the boundary to guesswork.
Replace adjectives with explicit lists: critical is SQL injection, XSS or CSRF; an error is a missing handler or a race condition.
Give the skip list real thresholds: no style, no linter-approved formatting, no snake_case complaints, no sub-5ms micro-optimisations.
Anchor each severity with a real code example, because prose severity drifts across runs and code anchors do not.
Three code-anchored examples beat a thousand-line description. The exam asks whether to write the vague prompt, and the answer is no.
steps.caption: Left describes the reviewer harder; right defines what qualifies. Same reviewer, one prompt change.
steps.why: The exam's tell is an option that adds a confidence adjective or a threshold instead of a boundary. 'Be thorough and conservative' is the prompt that produced the 47 findings, so keeping it and adding a prose rubric is the trap.
steps.contrast: Adding 'be thorough and conservative', or a five-level severity rubric described only in prose. It sounds more rigorous and produces exactly the same drift.
steps.exam: Any option whose content is 'be conservative', 'flag only high-confidence issues' or 'raise or lower the threshold' is a distractor. The first step is categorical criteria; few-shot examples refine them afterwards.
steps.takeaway: Do not describe the reviewer harder. Define what qualifies, what is an error, and what to skip.

steps.title: Gate: the first step to fewer false positives
steps.lead: The stem asks for the first step, and the options split into boundary-setting and threshold-fiddling.
steps.caption: Take the right exit: explicit criteria are the documented first step, not another adjective.

ask.q: A CI code-review bot flags about 50 items per pull request, mostly variable-naming opinions and micro-optimisations, and developers have started dismissing every finding without reading. The team wants to reduce false positives. Which approach is most effective?
options: Replace the vague instructions with explicit categorical criteria: what to flag, what each severity means, and what to skip, each anchored with a code example.
Add 'be conservative and only flag issues you are highly confident about' to the system prompt.
Add a five-level severity rubric described in prose so the model can weigh each finding before reporting it.
Instruct the model to assign a confidence score to every finding and report only those above 80 percent.
ask.why: Explicit categorical criteria are the documented first step: they turn a quality adjective into a boundary the model can apply. A conservative or high-confidence instruction is an adjective the model cannot calibrate to your codebase, a prose rubric has no code anchors and drifts across runs, and a self-reported confidence score is not calibrated to your project standards. Few-shot examples improve the criteria afterwards, but they are not the first step.

steps.takeaway: Categorical criteria first. Few-shot examples refine them, they do not replace them.

steps.title: Despite detailed instructions, output varies
steps.lead: The team already added the instruction to always include concrete fix suggestions, and the output is still sometimes detailed and sometimes vague. When a stem opens by telling you instructions have already failed, it is telling you the channel is wrong. Which technique actually fixes consistency?
points: Few-shot examples are the most effective technique for output consistency, not more instructions or a lower temperature.
Use 2-4 targeted examples on ambiguous scenarios. Not 1, not 10.
Each example shows input, output, and the reasoning for why that output is correct over plausible alternatives.
The reasoning is what makes the pattern generalise to novel cases.
steps.caption: Use 2-4 of these, not 1 and not 10. The bottom band is what carries the pattern to novel cases.
steps.takeaway: Consistency problem means 2-4 targeted examples with reasoning. Instructions grow linearly, edge cases combinatorially.
steps.inshort: When instructions alone produce variable output, the fix is 2-4 targeted few-shot examples with reasoning, not more instructions or a lower temperature.
steps.why: The stem says instructions have already failed, which means the channel is wrong; demonstration fixes consistency where description cannot.
steps.contrast: Adding more explicit requirements for each part of the format, or splitting into a two-pass instruction-only pipeline.
steps.exam: Consistency problem means 2-4 targeted examples with reasoning; instructions grow linearly, edge cases combinatorially.

steps.title: Gate: vague feedback, again
steps.lead: The bot finds real issues, but developers cannot act on them. The stem explicitly closes the door on one option before you start.
steps.caption: Look at the left column: the fix is a demonstration, not a more precise description.

ask.q: Automated reviews find real issues, but developers report the feedback is not actionable, with phrases like "complex ticket routing logic" or "potential null pointer" and no indication of what to change. Adding the instruction "always include concrete fix suggestions" still produces output that is sometimes detailed and sometimes vague. Which approach is most effective?
options: Refine the instructions further with more explicit requirements for each part of the feedback format.
Expand the context window to include more surrounding code so the model has enough information to propose concrete fixes.
Split into a two-pass approach where one prompt identifies issues and a second generates fixes.
Add 3-4 few-shot examples showing the exact required format: identified issue, location in code, concrete fix suggestion.
ask.why: Few-shot examples are the most effective technique when instructions alone produce variable output, because they demonstrate the required shape concretely rather than describing it abstractly. The scenario has already shown that more instructions do not converge; wider context does not constrain the shape of the feedback; and a two-pass split still relies on instruction-only prompting in each pass.

steps.takeaway: Show the shape. Do not describe the shape harder.

steps.title: Examples across varied structures
steps.lead: One more use of few-shot, and it is the extraction case. Three deployment triggers exist: detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent formatting, the model makes inconsistent judgement calls on ambiguous cases, and extraction produces empty or null fields for information that exists in the document. Here is the one people miss.
points: Few-shot reduces hallucination in extraction when examples cover varied document structures.
Cover inline citations versus bibliographies, narrative prose versus tables, and informal units.
The model learns the shape of a valid extraction instead of inventing data to fit the schema.
10 examples of one structure overfits to that structure. Use 2-4 examples spanning the structures you really receive.
For strict schemas, put format normalisation in the prompt: ISO-8601 dates, amount plus currency code, decimal fractions.
steps.caption: Cover the shapes you really receive: each spoke teaches what a valid extraction looks like.
steps.takeaway: Varied structures, few examples, with reasoning. The schema validates types; the prompt specifies formats.
steps.inshort: For extraction, few-shot examples must span the document structures you really receive, so the model learns the shape of a valid extraction instead of inventing data.
steps.why: Ten examples of one structure overfit to that structure; 2-4 spanning inline citations, bibliographies, prose, tables and informal units generalise.
steps.contrast: Giving many examples of the same familiar structure, which teaches pattern matching rather than the decision rule.
steps.exam: The schema validates types; the prompt specifies formats such as ISO-8601 dates and amount plus currency.

steps.title: Output tells what, reasoning tells how
steps.inshort: A few-shot example carries input, reasoning and output; the output shows what to produce and the reasoning shows how to decide, which is what generalises.
steps.lead: You already have 400 lines of prompt telling the CI reviewer what to do and not do, and it still labels the same bug critical on one run and high on the next. The model found the bug and reasoned about it correctly; it just did not use your team's label. A worked example fixes that, but only if it carries the reasoning.
points: An example is input plus reasoning plus output. The output tells the model what to produce; the reasoning tells it how to decide.
The answer is specific, but the reasoning behind it generalises, so the model extracts a decision rule and applies it to novel inputs.
Examples without reasoning teach pattern matching and restrict the model to the cases you showed, which is overfitting to familiar data.
Two to four examples is the sweet spot. Six to eight bloat the context and push the model back into pattern matching.
Find the fault lines first: run the same inputs several times, see where the output flips, and example only the drifting cases.
steps.caption: Row two is the anatomy: the output is specific, the reasoning is what carries the pattern.
steps.why: The exam claim is that few-shot examples are explicitly more effective than detailed prose, and the mechanism is the reasoning, not the output label. A test that asks why an example works wants the derivation.
steps.contrast: Giving input-and-label pairs with no reasoning, or filling the prompt with many examples of the cases the model already handles.
steps.exam: Ideal count is two to four targeted examples with reasoning. Five to eight fails on pattern matching and context bloating. In an agent, fix the tool description first.
steps.takeaway: Show input, reasoning and output. The output is specific; the reasoning is what generalises.

steps.title: Gate: the same bug, two different labels
steps.lead: Apply the anatomy you just read. The stem already told you more prose has not converged.
steps.caption: Read top to bottom: the first row is the fix; the rest are options the stem has already ruled out.

ask.q: A CI/CD review agent labels the same class of bug critical on one run and high on the next, even though the prompt has 400 lines of explicit rules. Which approach is most effective?
options: Add two to four targeted few-shot examples that show the reasoning for each severity boundary, then the label.
Add six to eight diverse examples for each severity so the model has more coverage of the label space.
Add detailed prose definitions of critical, high and medium to the existing instruction block.
Lower the temperature so the same input always produces the same label.
ask.why: Two to four targeted examples that carry the reasoning across the ambiguous boundary teach the decision rule and are the documented fix for inconsistent classification. Six to eight examples bloat the context and trigger pattern matching, prose definitions are exactly what already failed to converge, and temperature only removes randomness, not the judgement gap.

steps.takeaway: Two to four examples with reasoning on the boundary cases. Not more prose, not more examples.

steps.title: What tool_use actually guarantees
steps.lead: Slow down here, because this is the highest-yield task in the domain. `tool_use` with a JSON schema is the most reliable way to get structured output, and it eliminates JSON syntax errors such as malformed JSON, missing braces and trailing commas. That is the entire guarantee.
points: It does not guarantee semantic correctness.
Three failure modes survive the schema: arithmetic errors, field placement errors, and fabricated values.
Schema compliance is not source truth. Syntax validation is the first layer only.
Most distractors here are wrong-layer answers: asking the prompt to do the schema's job, or the schema to do validation code's job.
steps.caption: Everything under this root is a failure mode the schema cannot see; only the left child is fixed.
steps.takeaway: tool_use kills syntax errors. It does not kill arithmetic errors, wrong-field errors, or invented values.
steps.inshort: tool_use with a JSON schema eliminates JSON syntax errors and nothing else; arithmetic errors, field-placement errors and fabricated values survive it.
steps.why: This is the highest-yield task in the domain; most distractors are wrong-layer answers that ask the prompt to do the schema's job or the schema to do validation code's job.
steps.contrast: Assuming schema compliance is source truth, or asking tool_use to make line items sum to the total.
steps.exam: Syntax validation is the first layer only. Name the layer before the fix.

steps.title: Four layers, one job each
steps.lead: When a stem describes a failure, your first move is to name which layer is responsible. Almost every wrong answer moves the fix one layer away from the defect.
points: Prompt layer: format normalisation rules, because schemas validate types but not formats.
Schema layer: shape, presence, enum membership, nullability.
Validation layer: arithmetic, cross-field reconciliation, range and regex checks.
Source layer: whether the information exists at all. No earlier layer can manufacture it.
steps.caption: Read top to bottom: each layer can only fail in its own way, and only its own layer can fix it.
steps.takeaway: Name the layer before you name the fix.

steps.title: The fabrication factory
steps.lead: Here is the most dangerous schema decision you can make. An invoice extractor marks `purchase_order_number` and `payment_terms` as required with `strict: true`, and about 30% of the invoices do not carry a PO number. That schema just guaranteed the model will produce one anyway.
points: Required guarantees something will be present, not that it is true.
Strict mode requires `additionalProperties: false` on every object and every property listed in `required`.
Because `required` is not optional in strict mode, the anti-fabrication move is to make the field nullable.
Use a nullable type such as `["string", "null"]` and instruct the model to return null when the source does not state the value.
An all-required schema is a fabrication factory.
steps.caption: Left manufactures the value; right lets the model say null. Wording cannot override structural pressure.
steps.takeaway: Make it nullable and teach the model to say null. Prompt wording cannot override structural pressure.
steps.inshort: A required field whose value is often absent guarantees the model invents one; make the field nullable and teach the model to return null.
steps.why: Required guarantees presence, not truth, and strict mode still requires the field to be listed, so nullability is the only structural escape hatch.
steps.contrast: Adding 'do not fabricate' to the prompt while keeping the field required; wording cannot override structural pressure.
steps.exam: An all-required schema is a fabrication factory; nullable fields plus a null instruction are the anti-fabrication toolkit.

steps.title: Gate: required field, absent data
steps.lead: Apply the mechanism you were just handed. Note which option changes the structure and which ones change only the wording.
steps.caption: Take the right exit: the nullable field tells the truth instead of filling the gap.

ask.q: An invoice extractor marks `purchase_order_number` and `payment_terms` as required in its tool schema with `strict: true`. About 30% of invoices in the corpus do not carry a PO number. Field-level audits show the extractor returns plausible-looking PO numbers for exactly those documents, and downstream reconciliation fails. Which approach is most effective?
options: Add "do not fabricate values" to the extraction prompt while keeping both fields required.
Increase the retry limit so the model has more attempts to locate the PO number.
Run a second LLM call to verify every extracted PO number against the source.
Make both fields nullable by setting `type: ["string", "null"]`, and instruct the model to return null when the source does not state the value.
ask.why: A required field whose value is often absent is a fabrication factory: required guarantees something will be present, not that it is true. Nullable fields let the first call signal absence directly, which is cheaper and more honest than a verification pass that adds cost and can rationalise the original answer. Prompt wording cannot override structural pressure, and more retries produce more fabrications rather than more accuracy.

steps.takeaway: Change the structure, not the wording.

steps.title: tool_choice: four settings, one decision
steps.lead: Your shared intake service receives invoices, receipts, purchase orders and contracts with no reliable classifier. Each type has its own extraction tool and schema, prompt-based JSON sometimes returns prose and sometimes drops fields, and you need guaranteed schema-conformant output without knowing the type. That requirement picks the setting for you.
points: `auto`: the model may answer in text instead. Wrong when structured output is required.
`any`: must call some tool, and the model picks which. Correct for heterogeneous documents.
A named tool: must call this specific tool. Use it to mandate a first step or a single-tool workflow.
`none`: cannot call tools.
A named tool routes heterogeneous documents through one schema that fits none of them.
steps.caption: Read down the middle column: only 'any' guarantees a call while still letting the model choose the schema.
steps.takeaway: auto for optional, any for must-call-something, named tool for must-call-this, none to forbid.
steps.inshort: auto lets the model answer in text, any must call some tool and lets the model choose, a named tool must call that tool, none forbids tools.
steps.why: The requirement picks the setting: guaranteed structured output for an unknown document type means any, not a named tool.
steps.contrast: Forcing a named extraction tool for documents of unknown type, which routes every document through one schema that fits none of them.
steps.exam: auto for optional, any for must-call-something, named tool for must-call-this, none to forbid.

steps.title: Gate: unknown document type
steps.lead: Use the setting you just learned. The stem will tempt you with a single named tool because it sounds like a guarantee, but it guarantees the wrong thing.
steps.caption: The document is untyped at the door and typed by the time validation runs.

ask.q: A shared intake service receives invoices, receipts, purchase orders and contracts, and no reliable document classifier exists. Each document type has its own extraction tool with its own schema. Prompt-based JSON requests sometimes return prose and sometimes drop fields. The team needs guaranteed schema-conformant output for every document, without knowing the type in advance. Which approach is most effective?
options: Force `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"}` so the model always returns a schema-conformant object.
Keep `tool_choice: "auto"` and add "always respond with valid JSON" to the system prompt.
Set `tool_choice: "any"` so the model must call one of the extraction tools, then parse and validate the returned `tool_use.input` against that tool's schema.
Use one generic `analyze_document` tool with a free-text field and post-process the output into the per-type structure.
ask.why: `any` guarantees a tool call while letting the model choose the tool that fits the document, which is the correct pattern when the type is unknown and several schemas exist. A named tool routes every document through one schema that fits most of them; `auto` still allows an escape into prose; and a generic free-text tool reintroduces the inconsistent output shape the pipeline is trying to remove.

steps.takeaway: One tool that fits all types fits none of them.

steps.title: Enums, strict mode's edges, and what is gone
steps.lead: Three pieces of exact API surface the exam can test directly. A strict enum with no escape hatch creates validation failures when new categories keep appearing, strict mode does not support numeric range, string length or regex constraints, and assistant prefill is removed on modern models.
points: Add `unclear` to an enum so an ambiguous case has an honest option instead of a forced wrong bucket.
Add `other` plus a paired `_detail` string field to capture the source's own wording.
Supported in strict mode: `type`, `properties`, `required`, `enum`, `const`, `items`, `anyOf`, `$ref`, `additionalProperties: false`.
Not supported: `minimum`/`maximum`, `minLength`/`maxLength`, `pattern`, `oneOf`, `if`/`then`/`else`, recursive schemas.
For a direct JSON answer use `output_config.format` with a `json_schema` type; `client.messages.parse()` returns `response.parsed_output`.
steps.caption: The right column is the strict-mode surface that accepts the key and ignores the constraint.
steps.code:
strict: true  +  additionalProperties: false  +  every property in required
nullable field: "null if not found" via a null-capable type
enum: ["billing", "technical", "account", "unclear", "other"]  +  category_detail
output_config.format: {"type": "json_schema", "schema": {...}}
steps.takeaway: Nullable fields, unclear enums, other plus detail. Range and regex belong in code. Prefill is gone.
steps.inshort: Add unclear and other-plus-detail to enums, keep range and regex constraints in code, and use output_config.format because assistant prefill is gone.
steps.why: The exam can test the exact API surface: what strict mode supports, what it silently ignores, and which parameters are deprecated.
steps.contrast: Adding minimum, maximum, pattern or oneOf to the schema expecting enforcement, or using prefill to start the assistant turn with a brace.
steps.exam: Nullable fields, unclear enums, other plus detail. Range and regex belong in code. Prefill is gone.

steps.title: The fake tool that only enforces a schema
steps.inshort: A no-op tool whose only job is to accept a structured payload makes the API enforce your schema before the model's output reaches you.
steps.lead: Your tools return real data but in their own shapes: some integers, some strings, some nested objects. You want one structured record for the coordinator. The model will happily answer in markdown with the data wrapped in triple backticks, so the parser hits a backtick instead of a brace. The fix is a tool that does nothing but accept the payload you want.
points: The fake tool has no business logic. It exists so the API enforces the exact input_schema before returning data to you.
Free-form 'give me JSON' prompting is fragile: markdown wrapping breaks the parser and complex documents cause schema drift.
Read the result from response.content[0].input, the already-validated tool input, instead of parsing raw text.
Schema validity is syntax, not truth. A strict schema guarantees structure and nothing about whether the values are right.
Semantic errors survive it: reading the wrong table row, confusing similar terms, or hallucinating a value the source does not contain.
steps.caption: The hub does nothing; its job is to make the API enforce the schema before you parse anything.
steps.why: The exam separates syntax from semantics. Strict JSON schemas and tool use fix structural failures; business-logic checks, cross-field consistency and human review fix interpretation failures.
steps.contrast: Asking the prompt to return JSON without a schema, then post-processing markdown fences out of the text, which fixes the symptom and not the shape.
steps.exam: Structural failure means schema or tool use. Semantic failure means validation code. Do not answer a semantic stem with a stricter schema.
steps.takeaway: A fake tool is a typed contract. Schema validity is syntax; truth is a separate layer.

steps.title: Gate: schema perfect, value wrong
steps.lead: The stem gives you a pipeline that never fails schema validation, so the defect cannot be structural.
steps.caption: The pipeline passes every schema check, so the defect cannot be structural - take the semantic exit.

ask.q: An extraction pipeline passes JSON schema validation on 100 percent of documents, but occasionally reports wrong monetary amounts because the model reads the wrong table row. Which approach is most effective?
options: Add semantic validation: business-rule and cross-field consistency checks that compare the extracted values against each other.
Tighten the JSON schema further so the amounts are constrained to the expected range.
Route every document through the self-correcting retry loop until the amount stabilises.
Add a few-shot example showing the correct table row for every document layout you have seen.
ask.why: A schema-valid but wrong value is a semantic error, and only semantic validation catches reading the wrong row. A stricter schema changes structure, not interpretation, because range and cross-field constraints are not enforced in strict mode; the retry loop corrects formats, not interpretation, and would resubmit the same reading; per-layout examples do not generalise to the unseen layout that produced the error.

steps.takeaway: Schemas fix structure. Business logic and cross-field checks fix interpretation.

steps.title: Split the failure population first
steps.lead: A batch extraction over 8,000 contracts requires `governing_law` and `termination_notice_days`, and validation rejects 900. Sampling shows 700 of those contracts simply never state a governing law, while the other 200 use a date format the schema rejects. One number, two completely different problems, and the exam tests whether you notice.
points: The 200 are output errors. Retry fixes output errors.
The 700 are source gaps. No number of retries recovers information that was never in the document.
Memorise the sentence: retry handles output errors, schema design handles source gaps.
A field that is null because the contract does not state it is a correct extraction.
More retries on absent data produce more fabrications, not more accuracy.
steps.caption: The two segments need opposite treatments, so retrying all 900 as one population makes 700 fabrications.
steps.takeaway: Separate absence from format error before you decide anything.
steps.inshort: Separate output errors from source gaps before you decide anything: retry fixes output errors, schema design fixes source gaps.
steps.why: The stem deliberately mixes two failure populations in one number, and the correct option treats them differently.
steps.contrast: Retrying all 900 failures with the same prompt, which fabricates the 700 absent values and wastes the fixable 200.
steps.exam: Retry handles output errors. Schema design handles source gaps. Never retry an absent value.

steps.title: Gate: the 900 of 8,000 stem
steps.lead: Now answer it. The options differ in whether they treat both populations the same way or split them.
steps.caption: Row three is the trap: a single fix for both populations either fabricates or discards the fixable 200.

ask.q: A batch extraction over 8,000 contracts requires `governing_law` and `termination_notice_days` on every document. Validation rejects 900. Sampling shows 700 of those contracts simply do not state a governing law; the other 200 use a date format the schema rejects. Which approach is most effective?
options: Retry all 900 failed documents three more times with the same prompt.
Raise the retry limit from 3 to 10 for the failed documents.
Retry the 200 format failures with the source document, the failed extraction and the exact validation error, and accept null for the 700 documents where the value is genuinely absent.
Route all 900 failed documents to human review.
ask.why: The failures are two different populations and must be treated differently. Retry-with-feedback recovers output errors because the error message tells the model what specifically went wrong, while information that is absent from the source is not recoverable by retrying and needs a nullable field instead. Retrying everything produces fabrications, and escalating everything discards the majority that a targeted fix resolves.

steps.takeaway: Retry the format errors, accept null for the absent values. Never retry an absent value.

steps.title: Retry with feedback, and when to stop
steps.lead: So what exactly do you resend on a retry? Three things. Retry is effective for format mismatches, structural errors, misplaced values, locale-formatted numbers, and datetimes that need truncating to a date; it is ineffective when the information is absent from the source or lives in a document that was not provided.
points: Resend the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error.
A targeted correction beats a blind retry, and both beat `temperature: 0`, which only removes variability.
Recurring defect across many runs means a structural fix: add a few-shot example, make the field nullable, split the tool.
Prompt-level fixes generalise; per-instance retries do not.
A second call verifying every value adds cost and can rationalise the original answer. Use it as a sampling audit instead.
steps.caption: The cycle only works on output errors. Absence, or a document never provided, never comes back fixed.
steps.takeaway: Original document plus failed extraction plus the specific error. Recurring defect means structural fix.
steps.inshort: A retry resends the original document, the failed extraction and the specific validation error; a recurring defect needs a structural fix instead.
steps.why: Targeted correction beats a blind retry, and a prompt-level fix generalises where per-instance retries do not.
steps.contrast: Blind retries, temperature 0, or a second call verifying every value, which adds cost and can rationalise the original answer.
steps.exam: Original document plus failed extraction plus the specific error. Recurring defect means structural fix.

steps.title: Make a review bot measurable
steps.lead: One more stem shape for this task. A review bot's findings are dismissed 35% of the time, but the team cannot tell which categories drive the dismissals, so prompt changes are guesswork. What is missing is not a better instruction. It is a field.
points: Add `detected_pattern` plus `rule_id` or `evidence` to each finding, so dismissals aggregate by code construct.
Without it you know 35% are dismissed but not which constructs to suppress.
Extract both `stated_total` and `calculated_total` plus `totals_match`, so the mismatch surfaces for validation.
Routing fields: per-field `confidence` with `value`, plus `requires_review` and `review_reasons`.
steps.caption: Without detected_pattern you know 35% of findings are dismissed but not which constructs to suppress.
steps.takeaway: detected_pattern turns a black-box review bot into a measurable system.
steps.inshort: Add detected_pattern and a rule_id or evidence field to each finding so dismissals aggregate by code construct and prompt changes stop being guesswork.
steps.why: Without it you know 35% of findings are dismissed but not which constructs to suppress, so you cannot target the fix.
steps.contrast: Editing the prompt on instinct because the dismissals cannot be attributed to a category.
steps.exam: detected_pattern turns a black-box review bot into a measurable system.

steps.title: The self-correcting retry loop, and its limit
steps.inshort: A retry loop validates the output, appends the specific error to the conversation and asks again, and it corrects formats only, never absent data.
steps.lead: Your extraction runs, a validation gate checks the output, and it fails on a date in the wrong format. The loop appends that failure back into the conversation and calls the model again. Get this loop right and format errors converge; get it wrong and it spins forever producing the same failure.
points: Resend three things: the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error, appended in an assistant turn.
A generic 'validation failed' yields identical failures every time. Name the field and the expected format so the model can correct it.
The loop is a format corrector, not a data generator. It cannot recover information the source never contained.
If the value is genuinely absent, the fix is a nullable field, not another retry, and the loop should treat absence as success.
When the retry threshold is reached, hand off to a human rather than forcing the model to invent the missing value.
steps.caption: Follow the cycle to the bottom: it corrects formats and stops where the source holds no data.
steps.why: The exam tests the retry boundary repeatedly: retry fixes output errors, schema design fixes source gaps. A stem where every retry fails is a source gap, and an option that prompts the model to look harder is the trap.
steps.contrast: Resending the whole batch with the same prompt, or feeding back 'validation failed' with no field detail, which reproduces the same failure.
steps.exam: Retry sends the document, the failed extraction and the exact error. Recurring defect means a structural fix. Absence means nullable.
steps.takeaway: Retry with the specific error for formats. Absent data is never a retry problem.

steps.title: Gate: every retry fails on the same field
steps.lead: Read the stem for the word the retry loop cannot fix.
steps.caption: Left forces a value that does not exist; right lets the model report absence honestly.

ask.q: An extraction pipeline fails validation on every retry. The failing field is a tax ID that is genuinely absent from the source documents. Which approach is most effective?
options: Change the field to a nullable string, instruct the model to return null when the source does not state it, and treat null as a valid extraction.
Raise the retry limit and include the missing field in the feedback so the model looks harder for it.
Add a few-shot example of a document that does contain a tax ID so the model learns where to find it.
Fall back to a default tax ID value so downstream validation always passes.
ask.why: The value is absent from the source, so no number of retries can recover it; a nullable field lets the first call report absence honestly. Raising the retry limit and naming the field in feedback forces the model to invent a value, a few-shot example cannot create data that is not there, and a default value fabricates an identifier that the exam treats as a correctness failure.

steps.takeaway: Absence is a schema problem. Make it nullable; never retry an absent value.

steps.title: Batch is 50% off and takes up to 24 hours
steps.lead: Your manager says the Message Batches API is 50% cheaper and proposes moving both review workflows onto it. One is a pre-merge check that blocks developers until it completes; the other is a technical-debt report generated overnight for review the next morning. The question is never really about cost.
points: Message Batches API: roughly 50% cheaper, processing window of up to 24 hours, and no guaranteed latency SLA.
Design for the 24-hour worst case, not the typical case.
Right for high-volume, non-blocking, independent, deadline-flexible work: overnight reports, weekly audits, nightly tests.
Wrong whenever a human or a gate is waiting, and never migrate everything. The correct answer is the mixed strategy.
steps.caption: Read the middle column: a workload only tolerates the batch window when nothing is waiting on it.
steps.takeaway: Blocking means synchronous. Latency-tolerant means batch. Match the API to whether something is waiting.
steps.inshort: The Message Batches API is about 50% cheaper with a window of up to 24 hours and no latency SLA, so it fits non-blocking, deadline-flexible work only.
steps.why: The stem is never really about cost; it is about whether a human or a gate is waiting on the result.
steps.contrast: Migrating everything to batch, or batch with a synchronous fallback, which still queues the blocking job first.
steps.exam: Blocking means synchronous. Latency-tolerant means batch. Match the API to whether something is waiting.

steps.title: Where the batch window eats your deadline
steps.lead: The window is up to 24 hours and your downstream deadline is the SLA. What is left after the window is your buffer, and your submission cadence has to fit inside that buffer. Worked case: SLA 30h, window 24h, buffer 6h.
points: A record arriving just after a submission waits at most about 4h for the next batch, plus up to 24h processing.
That is about 28h against a 30h SLA. The constraint is start time plus 24h no later than the deadline.
The 4h is the submission interval, not an addition to the 24h cap.
SLA 36h with a 24h window allows roughly a 12h cadence. SLA 26h forces a 2h cadence.
Submitting once a day is only safe when the SLA is at least 48h, and the worst case is the slowest record.
steps.caption: Find the buffer first, SLA minus 24h, then choose a cadence that fits inside it.
steps.takeaway: Buffer equals SLA minus 24h, and the cadence must be shorter than the buffer.

steps.title: Drill: the manager's 50% proposal
steps.lead: Apply the split. Two workflows, one blocking and one overnight, and one option that sounds like it hedges.
steps.caption: The first two rows never move to batch, whatever the saving; the third one always does.

ask.q: Two workflows currently use synchronous calls: a blocking pre-merge check that must complete before developers can merge, and a technical-debt report generated overnight for review the next morning. The manager proposes moving both to the Message Batches API to save 50%. Which approach is most effective?
options: Move both to batch processing with a fallback to synchronous calls if the batches take too long.
Move both workflows to batch processing with status polling to verify completion.
Use batch processing only for the technical-debt report and keep synchronous calls for the pre-merge check.
Keep synchronous calls for both workflows to avoid any issues with batch result ordering.
ask.why: The 24-hour window with no latency SLA is acceptable for an overnight report and unacceptable for a gate that developers are waiting on, so the correct answer is the mixed strategy rather than all-or-nothing. A synchronous fallback still places the blocking job in the batch queue first, polling does not shorten the window, and avoiding batch entirely forfeits savings that the overnight report tolerates well. Result ordering is not a real constraint, because results are joined by `custom_id`.

steps.takeaway: A synchronous fallback only fires after the queue delay. The blocking job waits anyway.

steps.title: The one workload batch can never run
steps.lead: First, a workflow where the model calls a tool, sees the result, and continues cannot run on batch at all, which is a technical incompatibility rather than a latency problem. Second, results arrive in any order, so you join them by `custom_id` and never by position.
points: Multi-turn tool calling is not supported inside a single batch request, regardless of latency tolerance.
Batch does accept tool definitions in `params`. The block is executing them mid-request.
`custom_id` correlates request to response. Use stable unique identifiers so a partial re-run is straightforward.
Poll `batches.retrieve(id).processing_status` until it returns `ended`, then stream `batches.results(id)` as JSONL.
Resubmit only the failures identified by `custom_id`, and refine prompts on a sample before batching.
steps.caption: A loop that needs a tool result before continuing has no place to run inside fire-and-forget batch.
steps.takeaway: In-request tool loop means synchronous, always. Never batch the pre-merge hook.

steps.title: custom_id is an address, not a random UUID
steps.inshort: Every batch request carries a custom_id, and results come back in any order, so the ID is the only way to match a response to its request.
steps.lead: You submit a nightly batch of 500 files for review and, in the same batch, 500 files for test generation. The results arrive hours later in whatever order they finished. If a response cannot be traced back to its request, the savings are worthless. That is the job of the custom_id.
points: Every request needs a unique custom_id, and the result carries the same ID back, so correlation is by custom_id and never by position.
Make it meaningful, not a random UUID: a PR number, file path and version survive a partial re-run and a lost mapping.
The batch is processed asynchronously when capacity allows, so a submission can finish in minutes or in up to 24 hours.
Batch accepts tool definitions in params but runs single-turn only, so there is no in-request tool loop and no streaming.
Resubmit only the failures identified by custom_id after fixing the cause, not the whole batch.
steps.caption: The right column all assume position; only the custom_id survives results arriving in any order.
steps.why: The exam correlates batch request and response pairs, and the answer is always custom_id. A random UUID technically correlates but does not survive operational reality, which is why meaningful IDs are the documented choice.
steps.contrast: Matching results by their order in the batch, or using throwaway UUIDs that cannot be traced back to a PR or file.
steps.exam: Ask about correlating batch requests and responses and the answer is custom_id. Batch is single-turn; a tool loop means synchronous.
steps.takeaway: custom_id is the address on the shipment. Unique and meaningful, or you cannot rejoin the results.

steps.title: Gate: matching 500 results to 500 requests
steps.lead: The stem is about correlation, not cost.
steps.caption: The stem is about correlation, not cost - take the exit that echoes an identifier back.

ask.q: A nightly batch submits 500 review requests and 500 test-generation requests together. Results return hours later in an arbitrary order, and each must be matched to its request. Which approach is most effective?
options: Attach a unique, meaningful custom_id to every request and read the same custom_id from each result to rejoin them.
Keep the requests in submission order and match each result to the request at the same index in the results list.
Submit the two workloads as separate batches and rely on the batch creation order to tell them apart.
Include the file path at the start of each prompt and parse it back out of the response text.
ask.why: Results arrive in any order, so the only reliable correlation is the custom_id echoed on each result. Index matching assumes results preserve request order, which they do not; batch creation order says nothing about which result belongs to which request; and parsing a path out of free text reintroduces the fragile string handling that batch already avoids.

steps.takeaway: Join on custom_id. Never on position, batch order or parsed text.

steps.title: The model that wrote it cannot judge it
steps.lead: Non-obvious issues keep reaching production and are only caught when another team member reviews the PR. Someone reads the generation reasoning and finds the model considered those exact cases and concluded its own approach was correct. That is reasoning context bias.
points: A model reviewing its own output in the same session retains the reasoning context that produced it.
It is biased toward its prior conclusions and less likely to question its own decisions.
The fix is an independent instance: a fresh session receiving only the artifact and the criteria.
Self-critique instructions inside the generating session are the failure mode, not the fix.
steps.caption: Look at what crosses the arrow: the artifact and the criteria, never the reasoning that produced them.
steps.takeaway: Same session, same reasoning, same bias. Fresh instance, artifact and criteria only.
steps.inshort: A model reviewing its own output in the same session keeps the reasoning that produced it and stays biased toward its own conclusions.
steps.why: The fix is an independent instance receiving only the artifact and the criteria, the same reason human peer review works.
steps.contrast: Self-critique instructions inside the generating session, or deeper deliberation on the same chain of reasoning.
steps.exam: Same session, same reasoning, same bias. Fresh instance, artifact and criteria only.

steps.title: Gate: caught only by a colleague
steps.lead: Answer the stem you just read. Every wrong option keeps the same perspective in place and changes something else.
steps.caption: Every item on the right keeps one perspective in place and changes something else.

ask.q: Non-obvious issues such as performance optimisations that break edge cases, or cleanups that unexpectedly change behaviour, are only caught when another team member reviews the PR. The generation reasoning shows the model considered these cases and concluded its own approach was correct. Which approach is most effective?
options: Run a second independent instance to review the changes without access to the generator's reasoning.
Enable extended thinking for the generation stage so the model deliberates more thoroughly before producing suggestions.
Add self-review instructions to the generation prompt asking the model to critique its own suggestions before finalising.
Include full test files and documentation in the prompt context so the model better understands expected behaviour during generation.
ask.why: The model retained the reasoning context that produced the output and stayed biased toward its own conclusions, so the fix is a fresh instance with no generation history, which is the same reason human peer review works. More deliberation on the same chain of reasoning preserves the bias, self-critique instructions are the rationalisation loop that already failed, and extra context does not break a single-perspective bias.

steps.takeaway: Deeper deliberation on the same reasoning keeps the bias. Only independence removes it.

steps.title: Two passes: per-file, then cross-file
steps.lead: A pull request changes 14 files, and one pass gives detailed feedback on some files, shallow comments on others, misses obvious bugs, and flags a pattern in one file while approving identical code in the next. That is attention dilution. A larger context window does not cure it, because it is not a token problem.
points: Pass one is a per-file local analysis, which gives every file consistent depth.
Pass two is a separate cross-file integration pass for data flow, interface mismatches and boundary handling.
Single-pass review of 10 or more files fails on attention dilution and inconsistent standards.
Three full-PR passes carry three times the cost and the same dilution.
A bigger context window does not fix attention dilution, because it is not a token problem.
steps.caption: Trace one file down the per-file pass, then follow the cross-file arrows into the integration pass.
steps.takeaway: Split per-file for depth, then run a separate integration pass for cross-file issues.

steps.title: Confidence you can actually route on
steps.lead: Self-reported confidence is unreliable for routing, and an uncalibrated 0.9 means nothing: it is permissive in one system and prohibitive in another. Overall accuracy hides the rest, because a pipeline that is 97% accurate overall can be 80% accurate on one field or one document type.
points: Calibrate thresholds on a labelled validation set before raising an automation threshold.
Measure accuracy by segment: document type, field, source quality, confidence band.
Field-level confidence with a reason beats a bare score: `value`, `confidence`, `requires_review`, `review_reasons`.
Route to humans on low calibrated confidence, contradictory sources, high-impact fields and failed semantic validation.
Filtering low-confidence findings before developers see them hides findings instead of calibrating routing.
steps.caption: Note what is missing: overall accuracy is not the filter, and neither is a bare 0.9 score.
steps.takeaway: Calibrate on a labelled set and measure by segment. An uncalibrated threshold is meaningless.
steps.inshort: Calibrate thresholds on a labelled validation set and measure accuracy by segment, because an uncalibrated 0.9 means nothing and overall accuracy hides weak fields.
steps.why: Self-reported confidence is unreliable for routing; a pipeline that is 97% accurate overall can be 80% accurate on one field or document type.
steps.contrast: Setting a 0.9 threshold, or filtering low-confidence findings before developers see them, which hides findings instead of calibrating routing.
steps.exam: Calibrate on a labelled set and measure by segment. An uncalibrated threshold is meaningless.

steps.title: Domain 4 in one breath
steps.lead: That is Domain 4: twenty percent of the exam, six tasks, and one habit that ties them together. When a stem describes a failure, name the layer that failed before you name the fix, because almost every wrong option moves the fix one layer away from the defect.
points: Categorical criteria beat confidence adjectives. Flag X, report Y, skip Z, with each severity level anchored in a real code example.
Inconsistent output despite detailed instructions means 2-4 targeted few-shot examples with reasoning, across varied structures.
tool_use eliminates syntax errors and nothing else. All-required schemas are fabrication factories, so make fields nullable.
Retry fixes output errors, schema design fixes source gaps. Retry sends the document, the failed extraction and the exact error.
Batch suits flexible work, never a blocking gate or an in-request tool loop, and the instance that produced output must not review it.
steps.caption: Follow the chain: the wrong options all describe a fix that belongs one layer to the left or right.
steps.takeaway: Name the layer, then name the fix. That single habit answers most of Domain 4.
